To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) EPCs are reduced and delayed to be mobilized in T2DM after AMI, 2) this is related to impaired HIF/p-eNOS/p-Akt/MMP-9 pathway, 3) EPCs mobilisation is a predictor of cardiovascular events and mortality in T2DM and 4) EPCs may represent a therapeutic target in T2DM with AMI.

the mobilization of bone marrow-derived EPCs after AMI is delayed in T2DM and is accompanied by an impairment of bone marrow EPC signaling, which may contribute to the deterioration of cardiac function and worsen the clinical outcomes seen in T2DM.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the clinical relevance of bone marrow-derived EPC mobilization in T2DM and the underlying molecular mechanisms.
the clinical outcome of AMI patients with T2D, and with the role of impaired bone marrow EPC mobilization in this context.
the pathogenesis of diabetes and its complications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the impairment of the EPC mobilization is one of the mechanisms that may contribute to the worse clinical outcomes in AMI patients with T2D.
the impaired EPC mobilization and the impaired HIF/pAKT/p-eNOS signaling in bone marrow are the reasons for the worse clinical outcomes in AMI patients with type  2 diabetes mellitis.
diabetes impairs EPCs mobilisation, which in turn contributes to the worsening clinical outcomes in patients with AMI.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the worse outcome in T2DM is related to the impairment of bone marrow derived EPCs mobilizing capacity.
diabetes mellitus is associated with impaired EPC mobilization, which is associated with impaired cardiac function, increased ventricular remodeling and worse clinical outcome.

diabetes mellitus patients with AMI have impaired bone marrow EPC mobilization, which is related to the impaired signaling of HIF/p-AKT/p-eNOS and MMP-9, and this may contribute to the deterioration of cardiac function and worsen the clinical outcome of these patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
EPCs mobilisation may be a useful prognostic biomarker in T2DM.
the worse outcome in patients with TDM may be related, at least in part, to impaired EPCs mobilisation.
EPC mobilization is delayed in diabetes after AMI, and this may contribute to the worse clinical outcome in these patients.
